13830.title: Directional Light
13830.heading: Directional Light
13830.content:
A directional light models illumination whose rays share one direction and whose source is treated as infinitely far away. Unlike a [[Point Light]], it has no meaningful position and does not change direction across the scene.

Sunlight is a common use because the distance to the source is enormous relative to the game world. Surfaces respond according to their orientation toward the light direction.

13833.title: Disaster Recovery
13833.heading: Disaster Recovery
13833.content:
Disaster recovery restores data and computing services after a disruptive event. It is the technical recovery portion of a broader [[Business Continuity Plan]] and should be guided by a [[Recovery Time Objective]] and [[Recovery Point Objective]].

A secondary cloud or data center can provide recovery capacity, but recovery depends on current copies, compatible services, secure access, and practiced procedures. Merely possessing a backup does not prove that the complete application can be restored in time.

13836.title: Directional Gyro Wander
13836.heading: Directional Gyro Wander
13836.content: Gyro wander is a change between the indicated axis and the reference direction. Real wander comes from imperfections such as imbalance, friction, wear, or uneven rotor mass, while apparent wander comes from the observer's movement and Earth's rotation even if the gyro axis itself is ideal. A directional gyro must therefore be checked against the magnetic compass and periodically calibrated.

13839.title: Directional Derivative
13839.heading: Directional Derivative
13839.content:
A directional derivative measures the instantaneous rate of change of a multivariable function in a chosen unit direction $u$. For a differentiable function, it is $D_u f(x)=\nabla f(x)\cdot u$.

The [[Gradient]] supplies all such first-order directional information. Its direction gives the steepest local increase, while its negative gives the direction used by the [[Steepest Descent Method]].

13842.title: Directed Prompt
13842.heading: Directed Prompt
13842.content:
A directed prompt asks a focused question whose likely answers belong to a known set or semantic type. It communicates what information is needed and constrains the next recognition and understanding task.

Directed prompts can improve recovery by offering alternatives or examples. Overuse, however, turns a flexible assistant into a rigid [[Directed Dialog]] that prevents users from volunteering useful information.

13845.heading: Directed Minimum Spanning Tree
13845.content:
A directed minimum spanning tree restricts a learned Bayesian network to a tree-shaped dependency structure. Pairwise relationship weights identify a connecting tree, which is then oriented to obtain a directed probabilistic decomposition.

The restriction makes structure identification tractable and exposes important dependencies, but it cannot represent every pattern of interaction. Its simplicity is both the computational advantage and the modeling limitation.

13848.title: Directed Graph
13848.heading: Directed Graph
13848.content:
A directed graph is a [[Graph]] whose edges have directions. An edge from vertex $A$ to vertex $B$ does not imply that another edge leads back from $B$ to $A$.

The web is directed because one page may link to another without receiving a return link. Directed graphs can contain cycles, while a [[Directed Acyclic Graph]] prohibits them and is useful for dependency and prerequisite relationships.

13851.heading: Directed Acyclic Graph
13851.content:
A directed acyclic graph is a [[Directed Graph]] containing no [[Graph Cycle]]. It is commonly abbreviated DAG.

DAGs represent relationships that proceed in one direction without eventually returning to their starting point. Task priorities, prerequisites, and dependencies fit this structure when following the directed relationships can never lead back to an earlier item.

13854.title: Directed Dialog
13854.heading: Directed Dialog
13854.content:
Directed dialog structures an interaction around narrowly framed questions and expected answers. The assistant controls the sequence so that each turn supplies a known slot or decision.

The approach improves predictability for a [[Virtual Agent]] and can constrain a [[Speech Recognition Grammar]]. It becomes frustrating when users want to provide information out of order or take initiative.

A subset of endpoints or representative observations is usually more legible than labeling every point on every path.

A module P is a direct summand of a free module when there is another module Q such that P ⊕ Q is free. This means P can be included in a free module and recovered by a projection.

The condition characterizes [[Projective Module]]s. It permits projective modules to inherit many free-module properties without requiring them to possess a basis themselves.

Finite direct sums agree with direct products, but infinite sums retain the finite-support condition. A [[Free Module]] is a direct sum of copies of its base ring.

13866.title: Direct Proportionality
13866.heading: Direct Proportionality
13866.content: Two variables are directly proportional when $y=kx$ for a constant $k$. Multiplying $x$ by any factor multiplies $y$ by the same factor. A graph of $y$ against $x$ must therefore be a straight line through the origin, with gradient $k$; a straight line with a nonzero intercept is linear but not directly proportional.

13869.title: Direct Proof
13869.heading: Direct Proof
13869.content:
A direct proof of p → q assumes p and uses definitions, established results, and valid deductions to obtain q. For a universally quantified claim, the argument begins with an arbitrary member of the domain so that the conclusion applies to every member rather than a special case.

Direct proofs often succeed by translating abstract properties into their defining equations and then transforming those equations until the desired property becomes visible.

13893.heading: Diminishing Returns in Geometry Refinement
13893.content:
Diminishing returns in geometry refinement occur when additional detail or tighter repair produces less improvement in the decision-relevant result than the time, instability, and mesh cost it adds. The stopping point depends on the model's accuracy requirements and other sources of uncertainty.

A refined fillet is not valuable merely because it is more exact. Effort should move to material data, boundary conditions, validation, or another dominant uncertainty once geometry changes no longer affect the chosen outputs appreciably.

13896.heading: Direct and Indirect Game Actions
13896.content:
A direct game action changes an object or playspace through the player's immediate operation, such as moving a piece or aiming an avatar. An indirect action produces effects through a mediated system, delayed consequence, delegated unit, or chain of rules.

The distinction concerns causal distance, not importance. Indirect actions can create strategy by requiring the player to predict how a present decision will propagate through the [[Game State Snapshot|game state]].

13899.title: Diminished Reality
13899.heading: Diminished Reality
13899.content:
Diminished reality removes a selected real object from an augmented view and replaces its image region with a plausible view of what lies behind it. The system identifies the region of interest, obtains or reconstructs the hidden background, and composites that background over the object.

The hidden area may be observed from another time or viewpoint or modeled from surrounding evidence. Registration, changing illumination, and moving backgrounds determine whether the removal remains convincing.

13905.title: Dimension Reduction
13905.heading: Dimension Reduction
13905.content:
Dimension reduction maps observations from many measured coordinates into a smaller set of coordinates while attempting to preserve important structure. A two-dimensional representation can reveal sample relationships that cannot be plotted directly in the original space.

The preservation objective must be explicit: dominant variance, pairwise distance, class separation, and local neighborhoods are not identical goals. The source develops variance-ordered linear reduction through [[Singular Value Decomposition]].

13908.heading: Dimensional Analysis
13908.content: Dimensional analysis represents a physical quantity through powers of fundamental dimensions such as mass $M$, length $L$, time $T$, current $I$, and temperature $\Theta$. Every valid physical equation must be homogeneous: corresponding terms have the same dimensions. This requirement can detect algebraic errors and constrain the possible form of a relationship, although it cannot determine dimensionless numerical constants.

13914.content:
The dimension of a finite-dimensional vector space is the number of vectors in any basis of that space. Every basis has the same size.

Dimension counts independent directions, not the number of elements in the space. The dimension of a matrix's column space is its [[Matrix Rank]].

13920.title: Dijkstra's Algorithm
13920.heading: Dijkstra's Algorithm
13920.content:
Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest paths from one starting vertex to all other vertices in a graph with nonnegative edge weights. It initializes the start at distance zero and every other vertex at infinity.

The algorithm repeatedly selects the unvisited vertex with the smallest current estimate and applies [[Graph Relaxation]] to its neighbors. Recording each improved vertex's predecessor makes it possible to reconstruct a route after the final distances are known. Negative weights violate the assumptions that make a visited estimate final.

13923.title: Digital Surveillance
13923.heading: Digital Surveillance
13923.content:
Digital surveillance is the systematic monitoring and analysis of behavior through connected devices, platforms, sensors, or records. AI expands surveillance by recognizing patterns and identities at a scale that would be impractical for human observers.

The harm is not limited to disclosure of private facts. Continuous observation can change how people speak, move, associate, or work, especially when they cannot see the system or challenge its conclusions. The distribution of power matters: employers, companies, and states may gain detailed knowledge of individuals while remaining opaque about their own models and decisions.

13925.title: Digital Signature
13925.heading: Document

Status: #baby

Tags: [[.NET Cryptography and Access Control]] [[Applied Cryptography and PKI]]

13926.title: Digital Signature
13926.heading: Digital Signature
13926.content:
A digital signature uses a private key to sign data and a corresponding public key to verify the result. Verification provides evidence that the signed content has not changed and that the signer possessed the private key.

Practical signature APIs usually hash the message and apply an asymmetric algorithm such as RSA to the digest using a defined padding scheme. Trust in the signature still depends on securely associating the public key with the claimed identity.

Digital signatures support [[Nonrepudiation]] by giving a recipient verifiable evidence that the holder of a private key signed particular content. The public key checks that evidence, while a certificate or other trusted association is still needed to connect the key to a claimed sender.

13929.heading: Digital Service Integration
13929.content:
Digital service integration connects an assistant's conversation layer to systems that retrieve information or perform actions. Examples include calendars, weather services, messaging systems, commerce platforms, and smart-device controls.

The [[Dialog Manager]] converts an understood request into a service call, handles the result or error, and passes a symbolic response to [[Natural Language Generation]]. Conversation is therefore an interface to capabilities that usually live outside the assistant itself.

13932.heading: Digital Matte Painting with 2.5D Cards
13932.content: A matte painting can be separated into foreground, middle, and background images and staged as cards in depth. A camera move then gives their separation visible parallax while animation on individual cards supplies moving cars or other elements. In the book's environment examples, this arrangement can be mixed with genuinely modeled CG; the rendered environment may also be reduced to a single background plate when the camera angle permits. Choosing which features need real geometry is an efficiency decision governed by the desired shot, not by the source image's apparent complexity. See [[2.5D Depth Cards and Parallax]].

13935.title: Digital Paradigm
13935.heading: Digital Paradigm
13935.content:
The digital paradigm represents information, calculation, and control with discrete binary states. Arithmetic values, logical decisions, instructions, and transmitted messages can all be encoded as patterns of zeros and ones.

Its power comes from using a common representation across previously separate technologies. Once information is digital, the same electronic machinery can store, transform, copy, and communicate it.

13938.title: Digital Labor
13938.heading: Digital Labor
13938.content:
Digital labor is human work performed through or for data-driven platforms, including producing behavioral data, labeling examples, moderating content, and completing small online tasks. It often remains hidden behind descriptions of an AI system as autonomous.

Users can also supply economically valuable traces through ordinary participation without understanding their role in production. Ethical analysis asks who performs this work, who owns its products, how workers are compensated, and which risks are transferred to people with little bargaining power. [[Hidden Labor of AI]] is the portion most likely to disappear from the public story of automation.

13941.heading: Digital Input Device
13941.content:
A digital input device reports discrete states, commonly interpreted as on or off. Keyboard keys and gamepad buttons are examples, but useful game behavior usually requires more meaning than the current binary value.

Comparing present and previous states yields transitions such as just pressed and just released. Those transitions distinguish a single command from an action intended to continue while the control is held.

13944.sourceSearchName: digital image forensics digital image forensics
13944.title: Digital Image Forensics
13944.heading: Digital Image Forensics
13944.content:
Digital image forensics examines a photograph for evidence that its recorded history or visible content has been altered. It does not require a watermark or a signature embedded at capture; instead, it models the physical and computational stages that produced the image and tests whether their expected traces remain mutually consistent.

Those traces can occur in [[Image Metadata]], scene lighting and geometry, pixel statistics, camera-sensor artifacts, or [[JPEG Compression]]. Because each test rests on assumptions and has failure modes, a forensic conclusion should describe the particular evidence found rather than claim certainty from one detector.

13947.heading: Digital Game Distribution
13947.content:
Digital game distribution delivers a finished game electronically through an online store or portal. It removes physical inventory and retailer shelf constraints, allowing smaller teams and niche products to reach buyers directly.

The platform still takes a share, and the developer may have to fund discovery and marketing. Lower expected prices and a crowded catalog can offset the greater creative and logistical freedom.

13950.title: Digital Footprint and Data Shadow
13950.heading: Digital Footprint and Data Shadow
13950.content:
A digital footprint is the collection of traces associated with a person's activities across physical and online systems. The book distinguishes data knowingly made public from a data shadow: records gathered about a person without their knowledge, consent, or awareness.

Even deliberate sharing offers limited control once records are combined or repurposed. Likes, purchases, locations, and call metadata can support inferences about traits never disclosed explicitly. Privacy analysis must therefore consider what a dataset enables others to infer, not only what the original field appears to reveal.

13953.title: Digital Convergence
13953.heading: Digital Convergence
13953.content:
Digital convergence combines previously separate media and functions because they share binary representation and programmable processing. A single device can calculate, communicate, photograph, navigate, record sound, and display video.

Convergence depends on components becoming small, inexpensive, and interoperable enough to fit one system. Its direction is also shaped by design, regulation, markets, and user practices.

13956.sourceSearchName: digital audio sampling digital audio sampling
13956.title: Digital Audio Sampling
13956.heading: Digital Audio Sampling
13956.content:
Digital audio sampling measures a continuous sound waveform at regular time intervals and stores each measurement with finite precision. Sample rate determines how often measurements occur, while bit depth determines the available amplitude resolution.

Higher values can reproduce more detail but require more storage and transfer bandwidth. A game audio system balances fidelity, memory, decompression cost, and the importance of each asset.

13959.sourceSearchName: diffuse solar radiation diffuse solar radiation
13959.title: Diffuse Solar Radiation
13959.heading: Diffuse Solar Radiation
13959.content: Diffuse radiation is sunlight redirected by atmospheric molecules, vapor, dust, or clouds rather than arriving as a single direct beam. Ground-reflected diffuse light can also strike a tilted collector. It contributes to total [[Terrestrial Solar Radiation]], and a [[Flat-Plate Solar Collector]] can use it. Because it lacks one incoming direction, a mirror or lens cannot focus it like [[Beam Solar Radiation]].

13962.title: Diffraction Grating
13962.heading: Diffraction Grating
13962.content: A diffraction grating contains many equally spaced parallel slits. Their diffracted waves interfere to form narrow principal maxima satisfying $d\sin\theta=m\lambda$, where $d$ is slit spacing. More illuminated slits sharpen the maxima, allowing wavelength measurement and separation of spectral components with greater resolving power.

13965.title: Difficulty Mode
13965.heading: Difficulty Mode
13965.content:
A difficulty mode is a player-selected configuration that changes how much resistance a game presents. It can alter rules, resources, timing, enemy behavior, or other demands to create different pacing through the same underlying system.

Choosing a mode before play creates a paradox: the player may not yet understand the game well enough to know which setting will be satisfying. Multiple modes can also imply that one is the intended experience, so their effects should be made understandable and revisable where possible.

13967.sourceSearchName: differential scanning calorimetry differential scanning calorimetry
13967.title: Differential Scanning Calorimetry
13967.heading: Document

13968.sourceSearchName: differential scanning calorimetry differential scanning calorimetry
13968.title: Differential Scanning Calorimetry
13968.heading: Differential Scanning Calorimetry
13968.content:
Differential scanning calorimetry compares the heat required to drive a sample and a reference through the same temperature program. The difference reveals heat capacity as a function of temperature and can expose energetic transitions.

Differential temperature analysis uses a related comparison but records temperature differences to identify endothermic and exothermic behavior. The resulting measurements can populate the [[COMSOL Analytic and Interpolation Functions|functions]] used for realistic thermal properties and phase behavior.

13969.title: Differential Scanning Calorimetry
13969.heading: References

13971.title: Differential GPS
13971.heading: Differential GPS
13971.content: Differential GPS compares the satellite-derived position of a surveyed reference receiver with its known position. The difference estimates errors shared by nearby users, and broadcasting those corrections lets them improve their own solutions. Because satellite, clock, and some atmospheric errors are spatially correlated, differential techniques achieved ten-meter or better civil accuracy even under [[Selective Availability]] and much finer precision for surveying with suitable measurements and processing.

13974.title: Differential Rendering
13974.heading: Differential Rendering
13974.content:
Differential rendering computes how virtual content changes the appearance of a modeled real scene rather than replacing the real image with a fully synthetic rendering. A rendering with virtual contributions is compared with a rendering of the real-scene model alone, and their difference is applied to the camera image.

This preserves observed real detail while adding effects such as virtual shadows and reflected light. Its quality depends on sufficiently accurate geometry, materials, illumination, and registration.

13977.title: Differential Backup
13977.heading: Differential Backup
13977.content:
A differential backup copies files that changed since the most recent [[Full Backup]]. Each later differential grows to include every change accumulated after that common full snapshot.

Restoring the complete fileset generally requires the last full backup and the latest differential. This uses less storage than repeated full backups and fewer sets than a long incremental chain, while making individual-file location more complex than a single full set.

13980.title: Differential Analyzer
13980.heading: Differential Analyzer
13980.content:
A differential analyzer is an analog computer that solves differential equations by linking mechanical integrators. Vannevar Bush developed influential versions at MIT that represented mathematical relationships through rotating disks and shafts.

The machine supported scientific calculation and wartime firing tables. Its physical modeling approach also shaped proposals for electronic computers, even as digital numerical methods ultimately became dominant.

13983.sourceSearchName: difference of squares identity difference of squares identity
13983.title: Difference of Squares Identity
13983.heading: Difference of Squares Identity
13983.content:
The difference of squares identity is

$$a^2-b^2=(a-b)(a+b).$$

The two factors are conjugate binomials. When expanded, the cross terms (-ab) and (ab) cancel, leaving only the two squares.

The identity can be used in either direction for expansion, factorization, or exact calculation. Compound expressions may serve as (a) and (b), and repeated use can continue a factorization, as in (x^4-16=(x^2-4)(x^2+4)=(x-2)(x+2)(x^2+4)).

This depends on the two images aligning in camera, lighting, and exposure; unrelated changes can be mistaken for foreground. The clean plate also has another use in [[Wire Removal with Clean Plates]], where it supplies pixels behind an object removed by a roto window.

13989.sourceSearchName: difference of cubes identity difference of cubes identity
13989.title: Difference of Cubes Identity
13989.heading: Difference of Cubes Identity
13989.content:
The difference of cubes identity is

$$a^3-b^3=(a-b)(a^2+ab+b^2).$$

The sign in the linear factor matches the original difference, while every term in the quadratic factor is positive. Expanding the product cancels the mixed terms and leaves (a^3-b^3).

For example, (x^3-8=(x-2)(x^2+2x+4)). The identity is distinct from the [[Cube of a Difference Identity]]: (a^3-b^3) has two terms, whereas ((a-b)^3) expands to four.

13995.title: DIANA Splinter Group Implementation
13995.heading: DIANA Splinter Group Implementation
13995.content:
DIANA implements divisive hierarchy construction by selecting an unsplit cluster with large diameter and creating a splinter group. It first moves the record with greatest average dissimilarity from the remainder, then transfers other records when they are closer on average to the splinter.

The final two sets become child clusters and the process repeats. Splitting the largest-diameter cluster produces a monotonic hierarchy but remains sensitive to outlying records.

Tags: [[Character and Interactive Story Design]]

13998.title: Dialogue Tree
13998.heading: Dialogue Tree
13998.content:
A dialogue tree documents a scripted conversation as player choices and corresponding non-player-character responses. Each exchange can lead to another set of options, end the conversation, or trigger a game or story consequence.

The tree makes authored possibilities tractable without requiring unrestricted natural-language understanding. Designers must control branching growth and write options that accurately signal the avatar's intended meaning.

14001.title: Dialog Turn
14001.heading: Dialog Turn
14001.content:
A dialog turn is one participant's contribution before control passes to the other participant. In a voice interface, turn boundaries are inferred from speaking, silence, prompts, and interruption rather than explicit message submission.

The [[Dialog Manager]] uses turn state to decide when to listen, respond, wait, or accept an [[Interjection]]. Poor turn handling can make an accurate assistant feel slow or unresponsive.

14004.title: Dialog Transition
14004.heading: Dialog Transition
14004.content:
A dialog transition moves a finite-state interaction from one state to another after an event. Events can include a recognized user value, a no-match condition, timeout, help request, service result, or error.

Transitions make recovery behavior explicit in a [[Finite-State Dialog Manager]]. Their number can grow rapidly when every exceptional path is copied across many states.

14007.title: Dialog Policy
14007.heading: Dialog Policy
14007.content:
A dialog policy maps the current conversational state to the assistant's next action. The policy encodes choices such as whether to ask, confirm, execute, wait, or recover.

A policy can be hand-authored as a [[Finite-State Dialog Manager]] or learned through [[Reinforcement Learning]]. In either case, it must balance task completion, efficiency, error risk, and the user's interaction expectations.

14010.title: Dialog Module
14010.heading: Dialog Module
14010.content:
A dialog module is a reusable subflow for a recurring conversational function such as confirmation, help, authentication, or collecting an address. It packages related states and transitions behind a defined entry and exit.

Modules reduce duplication in a [[Finite-State Dialog Manager]] and make common recovery behavior consistent. They also expose clearer boundaries for testing and maintenance.

14013.title: Dialog Manager
14013.heading: Dialog Manager
14013.content:
A dialog manager chooses what an assistant should do next after receiving an interpreted user input. It combines the current [[Meaning Representation]] with conversation state, personal or display context, external results, and a [[Dialog Policy]].

Its actions can include asking for missing information, clarifying ambiguity, invoking a service, presenting a result, or recovering from an error. It therefore coordinates the other modules of the [[Virtual Assistant Pipeline]].

14016.title: Diagonalizable Matrix
14016.heading: Diagonalizable Matrix
14016.content:
A matrix is diagonalizable when it is similar to a [[Diagonal Matrix]]. Equivalently, it has enough linearly independent eigenvectors to form a basis.

If the eigenvectors form the columns of $Q$, then $Q^{-1}AQ=D$, where the diagonal of $D$ contains the corresponding eigenvalues. Repeated eigenvalues do not guarantee diagonalizability.

14019.title: Diagonal Matrix
14019.heading: Diagonal Matrix
14019.content:
A diagonal matrix is a [[Square Matrix]] whose off-diagonal entries are all zero. Its main diagonal can contain arbitrary values.

Diagonal matrices are inexpensive to multiply, invert when every diagonal entry is nonzero, and raise to powers. [[Matrix Diagonalization]] seeks a representation in which a matrix becomes diagonal because computations then reduce to independent scalar operations.

14025.title: Development Team
14025.heading: Development Team
14025.content:
A Development Team is the group that selects how to turn backlog items into a completed [[Product Increment]]. It plans and monitors its own work, adapts daily, and demonstrates the result rather than receiving a detailed task plan from a manager.

A game Development Team needs the disciplines required to deliver integrated, playable value. Shared accountability applies to the increment even when individual members retain specialties.

14028.title: Development Environment
14028.heading: Development Environment
14028.content:
A development environment is configured for creating and diagnosing an application. It may enable detailed error pages, verbose logging, development signing material, and tooling that should not be exposed publicly.

Environment-specific configuration can override general settings without changing production values. Publishing an application must explicitly select the intended [[Production Environment]] rather than carrying development diagnostics forward.

14031.heading: Developer Turnover Prediction
14031.content:
Developer turnover prediction estimates whether contributors are likely to leave a software project. Features can summarize activity hours, textual behavior, code readability, project conditions, and changes in participation.

The prediction unit and observation window must be explicit because inactivity can mean temporary absence rather than departure. Ethical use also requires caution when interpreting behavioral signals about individuals.

14034.heading: Deuterium-Tritium Fusion Reaction
14034.content: The deuterium-tritium reaction joins [[Deuterium]] and [[Tritium]] into a helium nucleus and a neutron. The source gives 17.6 MeV released per reaction and favors this pairing over the listed deuterium-deuterium reactions at its chosen operating conditions. 14037.title: Deuterium
14037.heading: Deuterium
14037.content: Deuterium is a hydrogen isotope whose nucleus has one proton and one neutron. The source identifies it as a naturally available fusion reactant obtainable from water. Paired with [[Tritium]], it can undergo the [[Deuterium-Tritium Fusion Reaction]] favored in the book's reactor discussion. Its abundance does not by itself solve the problems of plasma heating, confinement, and thermal-to-electric conversion.

14040.heading: Detrended Gene Expression
14040.content:
Detrended gene expression subtracts each feature's mean across samples so analysis emphasizes relative sample-to-sample variation rather than persistent differences in baseline expression among genes. The operation centers every gene row before sample correlations or principal components are calculated.

Centering helps global structure become visible, but it does not remove a [[Batch Effect]] by itself. It changes the reference level while preserving systematic deviations across samples.

14043.content:
Managed memory is reclaimed by garbage collection, but scarce operating-system resources such as file handles should be released as soon as their work is complete. Types that own such resources commonly implement `IDisposable` and expose a `Dispose` method.

A C# `using` statement or declaration guarantees disposal when control leaves its scope, including when an exception occurs. This produces predictable resource lifetimes and prevents open streams or handles from lingering until nondeterministic finalization.

14046.title: Deterministic Finite-State Automaton
14046.heading: Deterministic Finite-State Automaton
14046.content:
A deterministic finite-state automaton is a five-part machine (Q, Σ, q₀, δ, F): a finite state set, input alphabet, start state, total transition function, and set of accepting states. Every state-symbol pair selects exactly one next state.

The machine accepts a [[String]] when consuming the entire string from q₀ ends in F. Its states summarize only the finite information about the processed prefix that is relevant to future acceptance.

14049.sourceSearchName: deterministic context free language deterministic context free language
14049.title: Deterministic Context-Free Language
14049.heading: Deterministic Context-Free Language
14049.content:
A deterministic context-free language L is one for which a deterministic [[Pushdown Automaton]] accepts the strings of L followed by a distinct end marker. The marker lets the machine distinguish an actual end of input from a point where more symbols might still arrive.

Nondeterminism adds genuine recognition power to pushdown automata, so some context-free languages are not deterministic context-free. Deterministic context-free languages support efficient parsing methods such as [[LL(1) Parsing]] and [[LR(1) Parsing]].

14052.title: Determinant
14052.heading: Determinant
14052.content:
The determinant assigns a scalar to a [[Square Matrix]]. It changes sign when two rows are interchanged, scales when a row is scaled, and is unchanged when a multiple of one row is added to another.

A matrix is [[Nonsingular Matrix|nonsingular]] exactly when its determinant is nonzero. The determinant also appears in [[Cramer's Rule]] and the [[Characteristic Equation]], and for a triangular matrix it equals the product of the diagonal entries.

14055.heading: Designer Loop
14055.content:
The designer loop is the cycle in which a designer changes a game, observes players interacting with it, compares their experience with the design intent, and revises the design. It acts as a [[Balancing Loop]] around the [[Game-Player System]].

The loop cannot close through rules or a simulation alone; it requires actual player interaction. [[Prototype|Prototypes]] and [[Playtesting]] supply the evidence by which the designer reduces the gap between intent and experience.

14058.title: Design-Build-Test Loop
14058.heading: Design-Build-Test Loop
14058.content:
The design-build-test loop is an iterative production cycle in which a design is made tangible, tested, evaluated, and revised. All three activities overlap throughout development even though their relative emphasis changes over time.

Early iterations focus on concept and fast prototypes, production shifts toward implementation, and later work emphasizes testing and correction. Keeping the loop short makes uncertainty visible before it becomes expensive and supplies evidence for the [[Designer Loop]].

14061.heading: Design-Oriented Computational Thinking
14061.content:
Design-oriented computational thinking constructs virtual worlds in which people can achieve meaningful purposes. It combines technical knowledge with sensitivity to user practices, concerns, history, identity, and assessments of quality.

It includes software engineering rather than replacing it. Correctness and reliability establish a foundation, while contextual inquiry and iterative feedback determine whether the system creates value.

14064.title: Designer-Based Balancing
14064.heading: Designer-Based Balancing
14064.content:
Designer-based balancing uses the designer's learned heuristics and intuition to judge whether relationships and progression feel appropriate. It is especially useful early, before enough playable material or behavioral data exists.

Intuition can guide promising hypotheses but is unreliable as sole evidence. Competing intuitions are better resolved through a fast [[Prototype]], mathematical model, or [[Playtesting|playtest]] than through prolonged argument.

14067.title: Design Value Alignment
14067.heading: Design Value Alignment
14067.content:
Design-value alignment is the shared understanding that lets collaborators evaluate a game against the same intended qualities. It gives a team a reason for choosing one mechanic, representation, or compromise over another when several options are feasible.

Alignment does not require identical solutions or eliminate creative autonomy. It establishes common criteria so that disagreement can focus on which proposal best advances the intended player experience.

14070.title: Design Values
14070.heading: Design Values
14070.content:
Design values are explicit qualities the finished play experience should embody. They describe what the team is trying to make players do, perceive, consider, and feel rather than enumerating features that happen to be present.

Because values remain stable while implementations change, they guide choices throughout iteration. A proposed feature is useful when it advances those qualities and expendable when it does not.

14073.title: Design Values as Exit Criteria
14073.heading: Design Values as Exit Criteria
14073.content:
Design values become exit criteria when the team uses them to judge whether iteration has produced the intended experience consistently enough to proceed. This converts broad creative aspirations into questions that evidence from playtests can answer.

A feature-complete game can still fail this test if its play contradicts the agreed qualities. Conversely, a simpler implementation may be ready when it fulfills the values without requiring additional design complexity.

14076.title: Design Revision Decision
14076.heading: Design Revision Decision
14076.content:
A design revision decision chooses which evaluated response will enter the next prototype. It weighs fit with design values, expected effect, cost, risk, dependencies, and what the revision will make possible to learn.

The decision should also record what is deliberately not being changed. This protects a focused test from accumulating unrelated improvements that obscure whether the chosen response worked.

14079.title: Design Matrix
14079.heading: Design Matrix
14079.content:
A design matrix places one experimental unit in each row and one modeled term in each column. Its entries encode the intercept, group indicators, continuous predictors, transformations, and interactions used to explain the outcome vector.

The matrix is both a mathematical and scientific specification. Choosing its columns determines which coefficients can be estimated and what each one means; R's `model.matrix` exposes the representation generated from a model formula.
